title: What is a king tide, and how could it make conditions worse along B.C.'s coast? | CBC News
html:
Science·New

How king tides happen, and what that means amid flood warnings in B.C.

King tides can be around half a metre higher than average high tide levels, lasting for a few days

Officials on the West Coast of Canada and the U.S. are warning those living close to the ocean about potential flooding, thanks in part to what's called a king tide.

This perfect storm of alignment between Earth, the moon and the sun can create dramatic tides that can be about 0.3 to 0.6 metres higher than the average high tide mark.

The current king tide is expected to end on Thursday, but up until then, officials are warning people along the coast about the potential of flooding, as these higher-than-normal tides coincide with sea level rise caused by El Niño.

Oceanographer Gregory Crawford says this is a "worst-case scenario."

"Certainly low-lying places that don't have a lot of sea wall protection and such are going to potentially have some worse flooding than you would normally have," said Crawford, an adjunct professor at Ontario Tech University in Oshawa, Ont.

According to the Weather Network, current forecasts expect the highest tide on Wednesday morning, coinciding with the full moon.

A bus moves through floodwaters during high tides on Tuesday in Sausalito, Calif. (Heather Diehl/The Associated Press)

How does a king tide happen?

There are a few different types of alignments that can produce higher-than-normal tides.

Tides are caused by the push and pull of the moon and sun on the ocean. As those celestial bodies shift, so do the tides.

There are spring tides, which happen every two weeks when the moon and sun align on the same side of Earth, resulting in tides that are about 20 per cent higher than normal.

There is also the perigean tide, which happens three or four times a year, when the moon is at its closest approach to Earth in its orbit.

When both of these alignments happen at once, you get the king of all tides, which typically happens in the late fall and early winter and can last for a few days.

"Essentially, the pull of the moon and the pull of the sun line up to kind of maximize the tidal range that you get. And that's what we call the king tide," said Crawford.

Tides predictable, storms are not

Crawford says these king tides are fairly predictable, as it's all astronomy, with the most dramatic conditions lasting for just a few days, so those close to the water know when to expect them.

And while the king tides themselves aren't overly dangerous, it's important to watch out for what else is going on around the ocean.

"When you get El Niño and king tides and weather, and/or tsunamis, when they all add up together, that can be a lot more serious," said Crawford.

Waves are pictured crashing into the seawall in English Bay during a king tide in Vancouver on Jan. 7, 2022. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

Crawford says king tides aren't typically on the mind of those who live inland, but if you spend time on the water, chances are you know about these more dramatic tides.

"If you're kind of up on a hill, you're probably not so worried about it," said Crawford.

Crawford says these king tides happen about two to four times a year.

According to the Weather Network, B.C. can expect more king tides next month, from Dec. 22-26.
summary: This perfect storm of alignment between Earth, the moon and the sun can create dramatic tides that can be about a metre higher than the average high tide mark.
